title: Projectile motion
subtitle: Predict a flight, change its launch, and explain the result.
objectives: Explain how changing speed changes flight time, horizontal range, and maximum height.
Compare complementary launch angles and explain their equal range under the model assumptions.
Identify why air resistance or unequal launch and landing heights can change these conclusions.
assumptions: Two-dimensional motion with constant downward gravity g = 9.81 m/s² and no air resistance.
Launch and landing are at the same height. Speed is 0–50 m/s; angle is 0–90 degrees from horizontal.
Horizontal motion has constant velocity; vertical motion has constant acceleration. Flight ends on returning to launch height.
With zero speed or a horizontal launch from ground level, the flight duration, range, and height are zero. A vertical launch has zero range.

questions.question: At a fixed angle of 30°, what happens to flight time, range, and maximum height if speed doubles? Predict, then compare 20 and 40 m/s.
questions.answer: Flight time doubles, while range and maximum height each quadruple. Time is proportional to speed; range and height are proportional to speed squared when the angle and gravity stay fixed.

questions.question: At the same nonzero speed, do 30° and 60° give the same range? Which flight lasts longer and reaches higher?
questions.answer: They have equal range because sin(2 × 30°) = sin(2 × 60°). The 60° launch has more initial upward velocity, so it lasts longer and reaches higher. Complementary angles sum to 90°.

questions.question: Must complementary angles still have equal range with air resistance or different launch and landing heights?
questions.answer: No. The equal-range relationship depends on this model's no-drag and equal-height assumptions. Drag changes the velocities during flight; unequal heights change the landing time. These situations require a different model.
